items.prompt: What is the merge base?
choices: The most recently modified file in the entire repository's commit history
The last commit both branches share before they diverged
The branch that currently has the most total commits recorded against it
Whichever branch happened to be created first in the repository's history
items.explanation: The merge base is the shared ancestor commit — the point where the two branches' histories split. Git needs it to tell what each branch actually changed.
items.reference:
Merge base
📍 the last commit both branches share
🌿 Alex's branch → diverges here
🌿 Sam's branch → diverges here

Why: git diffs each branch against this shared commit separately — that's what lets it tell "Alex changed this" apart from "Sam changed this."

items.prompt: Why does git need a merge base at all instead of just comparing the two branches to each other?
choices: It doesn't — a direct comparison between the two branches would work exactly as well
The merge base lets git attribute each change to whoever made it, not just see that the files disagree
The merge base is only ever consulted during a fast-forward merge, never a real one
The merge base is what determines which collaborators have commit permissions on a branch
items.explanation: A direct two-way diff only shows that two files disagree, with no way to know who caused the disagreement. Comparing each branch against the shared base is what makes attribution possible.
items.reference:
Merge base
📍 the last commit both branches share
🌿 Alex's branch → diverges here
🌿 Sam's branch → diverges here

Why: git diffs each branch against this shared commit separately — that's what lets it tell "Alex changed this" apart from "Sam changed this."

items.prompt: Alex adds a line near the top of a file; Sam edits a line near the bottom of the same file, on a different branch. What happens on merge?
choices: Automatic conflict, since both branches touched the same file
Auto-merge — both changes are combined with no conflict
Whichever branch merges second silently wins, no message shown
Git refuses to merge files that were both edited
items.explanation: Conflicts are decided at the line level, not the file level. Different lines touched on each side means both changes combine automatically.
items.reference:
Auto-merge condition
🟢 different lines touched → auto-merge
🔴 same line, different content → conflict

Why: Git compares which lines each side's diff actually touched — not which file, and not how many lines.

items.prompt: What actually determines whether a merge needs human help?
choices: How many total files were changed across both branches combined
Whether the two branches changed the exact same line to different content
Which branch happens to have a more descriptive, detailed commit message attached
The total number of commits recorded on each branch before the merge
items.explanation: The deciding factor is line-level overlap with differing content — not file count, commit count, or anything about commit messages.
items.reference:
Auto-merge condition
🟢 different lines touched → auto-merge
🔴 same line, different content → conflict

Why: Git compares which lines each side's diff actually touched — not which file, and not how many lines.

items.prompt: Alex and Sam both independently change the same constant to the exact same new value on their branches. What happens on merge?
choices: Conflict — any line touched by both branches always conflicts, regardless of the content
Auto-merge — since both sides agree on the new content, there's nothing to ask
Git picks whichever branch is labeled 'ours' and silently discards the other side's edit
The file is left completely unchanged and both branches' edits to it are dropped
items.explanation: A conflict requires the same line to be changed to *different* content on each side. Identical edits from both sides merge cleanly.
items.reference:
Real conflict, precisely
same base line
changed by both sides
to different content

Why: If both sides change a line to the same new content, git doesn't ask — they agreed, nothing to resolve.

items.prompt: Which of these is a genuine merge conflict?
choices: Both branches add different new functions to different parts of the file
Both branches change the same line's value to two different numbers
One branch adds a comment; the other renames a variable elsewhere
Both branches leave a particular line completely untouched
items.explanation: Only the case where the same base line is changed to two different pieces of content on each side forces a real conflict.
items.reference:
Real conflict, precisely
same base line
changed by both sides
to different content

Why: If both sides change a line to the same new content, git doesn't ask — they agreed, nothing to resolve.

items.prompt: What does the `=======` line inside a conflict marker block represent?
choices: The marker denoting the end of the entire file, after which nothing else is read
The dividing line between 'our' version and 'their' version of the conflicting content
A syntax error that the compiler or interpreter will reject until it's deleted
The original, pre-conflict version of the line as it existed at the merge base
items.explanation: `=======` separates the two conflicting versions shown between `<<<<<<<` and `>>>>>>>` — everything above it is 'ours,' everything below is 'theirs.'
items.reference:
Conflict markers
<<<<<<< ours — your branch's version
======= — the dividing line
>>>>>>> theirs — the other branch's version

Why: Both full versions are shown inline in the file itself, so you can edit, pick one, or combine them by hand.

items.prompt: After git inserts conflict markers into a file, what is the developer expected to do?
choices: Nothing — git resolves the conflict automatically after a short delay on its own
Edit the file to remove the markers and leave the correct final content, then mark it resolved
Delete the entire file from the repository and recreate it from scratch
Revert both branches all the way back to the shared merge base commit
items.explanation: Conflict markers are a prompt for a human decision — edit the file down to the intended final content (from either or both sides) and remove the markers before completing the merge.
items.reference:
Conflict markers
<<<<<<< ours — your branch's version
======= — the dividing line
>>>>>>> theirs — the other branch's version

Why: Both full versions are shown inline in the file itself, so you can edit, pick one, or combine them by hand.

items.prompt: What makes a merge a 'fast-forward' merge?
choices: It happens faster than a normal merge purely as a matter of execution timing
The branch being merged into hasn't diverged — it's still exactly at the merge base
Both branches happened to change exactly the same set of lines in the file
The merge was triggered using a keyboard shortcut instead of a typed command
items.explanation: Fast-forward specifically means the receiving branch has no commits of its own since the split — git just moves its pointer forward, no reconciliation needed.
items.reference:
Fast-forward merge
receiving branch hasn't moved
→ pointer just moves forward
no merge commit created

Why: No independent history exists on the receiving side, so there's nothing to reconcile — just relabel where the branch points.

items.prompt: Does a fast-forward merge ever produce a real merge conflict?
choices: Yes, whenever the two branches happen to touch the same file during the merge
No — there's no independent history to compare, so nothing can conflict
Only if the file involved is larger than some threshold size git enforces
Yes, but this only ever happens for binary files, never plain text
items.explanation: A fast-forward has no divergent history on the receiving side to compare against — the three-way comparison that produces conflicts never runs.
items.reference:
Fast-forward merge
receiving branch hasn't moved
→ pointer just moves forward
no merge commit created

Why: No independent history exists on the receiving side, so there's nothing to reconcile — just relabel where the branch points.

items.prompt: What problem does comparing against a merge base solve that a direct branch-to-branch diff can't?
choices: It makes the underlying diff computation run measurably faster for git internally
It lets git tell which branch actually made each change, instead of just seeing two files disagree
It removes the need for conflict markers to ever appear in a merged file
It only matters when merging binary files, not ordinary text source files
items.explanation: A direct diff between two branches shows a disagreement but not its cause. Diffing each branch against the shared base attributes every change to whoever made it.
items.reference:
Why three-way, not two-way
base → ours = Alex's real changes
base → theirs = Sam's real changes
compare those two change lists

Why: A raw ours-vs-theirs diff can only show disagreement, not who caused it — that's the whole reason the base is needed.

items.prompt: In a three-way merge, how many diffs does git actually compute?
choices: One — git computes a single diff directly between the two branches themselves
Two — base against each branch — then those two change lists are compared to each other
Three — one diff per branch, plus a third diff against the final merge result
Zero — git relies entirely on manual inspection by a human, with no diff at all
items.explanation: Two diffs (base→ours, base→theirs) produce two independent change lists, which git then reconciles line by line.
items.reference:
Why three-way, not two-way
base → ours = Alex's real changes
base → theirs = Sam's real changes
compare those two change lists

Why: A raw ours-vs-theirs diff can only show disagreement, not who caused it — that's the whole reason the base is needed.

items.prompt: Sam's branch deletes a line that Alex's branch never touched. What does the three-way merge conclude?
choices: Conflict — any line deletion on either branch always requires a human to review it
The line is removed in the merged result, since only theirs changed it and ours kept it
The line is kept in the result, since deletions are always ignored by three-way merges
Git refuses to merge the branches at all once any deletion is present on either side
items.explanation: Only one side changed (deleted) this line while the other kept it — that's a one-sided change, which auto-merges by taking the side that changed it.
items.reference:
Why three-way, not two-way
base → ours = Alex's real changes
base → theirs = Sam's real changes
compare those two change lists

Why: A raw ours-vs-theirs diff can only show disagreement, not who caused it — that's the whole reason the base is needed.

items.prompt: A direct two-way diff between Alex's and Sam's files shows line 4 differs. What can it NOT tell you?
choices: That line 4 is actually different between the two files being compared
Which side actually changed line 4, versus which side is the original
The exact byte-for-byte content of line 4 as it appears in each file
That the two files being compared have a different total number of lines
items.explanation: A two-way diff only reports disagreement, not causation — it has no third reference point (the base) to know which side actually moved away from the original.
items.reference:
Two-way vs. three-way
two-way: 'these files disagree'
three-way: 'here is exactly what each side changed'

Why: Attribution, not just detection, is the thing a raw two-way diff can never give you.

items.prompt: Why can't a two-way diff safely auto-merge non-overlapping changes either?
choices: It actually can do this safely — three-way comparison isn't needed for that simpler case
Without knowing what changed relative to a shared base, it can't tell 'this is new' from 'this was always different'
Two-way diffs are inherently and measurably slower to compute than three-way diffs
Two-way diffs only ever work correctly when comparing binary files, not text
items.explanation: Even the 'easy' auto-merge case depends on knowing what each side changed relative to a common starting point — which only the base comparison provides.
items.reference:
Two-way vs. three-way
two-way: 'these files disagree'
three-way: 'here is exactly what each side changed'

Why: Attribution, not just detection, is the thing a raw two-way diff can never give you.

items.prompt: Per the merge procedure in L2, what happens when only Alex's branch changed a base line and Sam's branch left it alone?
choices: Conflict, since any change made to a line shared by both branches requires manual review
Alex's version of that line is taken, with no conflict
The original base line is kept as-is, and Alex's change to it is simply ignored
The line is deleted entirely from the merged result, regardless of either branch's content
items.explanation: A one-sided change (only one branch touched the line) auto-merges by taking whichever side made the change.
items.reference:
Per base line, per side
neither changed → keep base
one changed → take that side
both changed, differ → conflict
both changed, same → take it, no conflict

Why: The exact same four-way branch runs for every line in the base file.

items.prompt: Per the merge procedure, when do conflict markers actually get inserted?
choices: Whenever both branches happen to touch the same file, regardless of which specific lines
Only when both branches changed the same base line to different content
Whenever a branch involved in the merge has accumulated more than ten commits
Whenever the file being merged exceeds some fixed size threshold git enforces
items.explanation: The procedure only branches into a conflict when both sides changed the same line AND their replacements actually differ.
items.reference:
Per base line, per side
neither changed → keep base
one changed → take that side
both changed, differ → conflict
both changed, same → take it, no conflict

Why: The exact same four-way branch runs for every line in the base file.

items.prompt: Alex and Sam both independently fix the same bug on the same line, landing on identical corrected code. Does this conflict?
choices: Yes — two branches touching the same line is always treated as a conflict, period
No — since the replacement content is identical on both sides, there's nothing to resolve
Only if they also happened to rename a local variable somewhere else in the file
Yes, but only in cases where the matching fix spans more than a single line
items.explanation: The merge only flags a conflict when the two sides' replacements for the same line actually differ. Identical replacements merge silently.
items.reference:
Identical edits
Alex changes TAX_RATE → 0.0825
Sam changes TAX_RATE → 0.0825
same target value → no conflict

Why: The merge logic explicitly compares the two replacement contents before deciding there's anything to ask about.

items.prompt: Why does this behavior matter in practice for teams working on the same codebase?
choices: It doesn't actually come up often enough in real codebases to matter much
It means independently converging on the same fix (e.g. both applying a linter's suggested change) won't create needless manual work
It means git will silently and arbitrarily pick one of the two matching edits at random
It only ever applies to pure whitespace changes, never to substantive code edits
items.explanation: This is exactly what saves a team from an unnecessary conflict resolution step when two people independently arrive at the same correct fix.
items.reference:
Identical edits
Alex changes TAX_RATE → 0.0825
Sam changes TAX_RATE → 0.0825
same target value → no conflict

Why: The merge logic explicitly compares the two replacement contents before deciding there's anything to ask about.

items.prompt: What specifically does the merge algorithm compare to decide 'identical edit, no conflict' versus 'real conflict'?
choices: The commit messages left on each branch describing why the change was made
The exact replacement content each side produced for that line (or insertion)
The exact timestamp recorded for each change on either branch
The author name attached to the commit that introduced each change
items.explanation: The comparison is purely over the actual line content each side produced — nothing about commit metadata factors into the decision.
items.reference:
Identical edits
Alex changes TAX_RATE → 0.0825
Sam changes TAX_RATE → 0.0825
same target value → no conflict

Why: The merge logic explicitly compares the two replacement contents before deciding there's anything to ask about.

items.prompt: Sam's branch has zero commits of its own since branching from Alex's. Sam merges Alex's branch in. What happens?
choices: A merge commit is always created by git, regardless of whether real divergence exists
Fast-forward — Sam's branch pointer just moves to match Alex's latest commit, no merge commit
Git refuses the merge outright, since Sam's branch is considered 'empty' with no commits
A conflict is generated automatically the moment git notices zero commits on one side
items.explanation: With no divergent history on Sam's side, there's nothing to reconcile — git simply advances the pointer, producing no merge commit.
items.reference:
Fast-forward vs. true merge
fast-forward: pointer moves, no new commit
true merge: independent history on both sides → merge commit created

Why: Whether a merge commit appears at all depends entirely on whether real divergence exists to reconcile.

items.prompt: Why does a true (non-fast-forward) merge produce a merge commit, but a fast-forward doesn't?
choices: Merge commits are just a cosmetic configuration setting, unrelated to actual divergence
A merge commit records how two independently-diverged histories were reconciled — with no divergence, there's nothing to record
Fast-forward merges are actually slower to perform, so git skips the commit purely to save time
Merge commits only ever get created specifically when a real conflict has occurred
items.explanation: A merge commit exists specifically to capture the reconciliation of two divergent histories. When one side never diverged, there's no reconciliation event to record.
items.reference:
Fast-forward vs. true merge
fast-forward: pointer moves, no new commit
true merge: independent history on both sides → merge commit created

Why: Whether a merge commit appears at all depends entirely on whether real divergence exists to reconcile.

items.prompt: Why does keeping branches short-lived actually reduce merge conflicts, mechanically?
choices: Short-lived branches are simply exempt from running the three-way merge algorithm at all
Less time and fewer touched lines means lower odds that another branch's change list overlaps with yours on the same lines
Git enforces a hidden internal time limit after which any pending merge is forced to succeed
It doesn't actually reduce conflicts in practice at all — that claim is really just a myth
items.explanation: Conflict risk is driven by line-level overlap between two independent change lists — shorter branches touch fewer lines over less time, directly lowering that overlap.
items.reference:
Branch lifetime and risk
longer-lived branch
→ more lines touched
→ more time for others to touch the same lines
→ higher line-overlap odds

Why: This is a mechanical consequence of the merge procedure, not a rule of thumb without a cause.

items.prompt: Two branches each touch 5% of a file's lines, chosen independently. A third pair of branches each touch 40% of the same file. Which pair is more likely to hit a genuine conflict?
choices: Both pairs are equally likely to conflict — the percentage of lines touched doesn't actually matter
The 40%-each pair, since more touched lines raises the odds their change lists overlap
The 5%-each pair, since smaller, more surgical changes are actually harder for git to merge cleanly
Neither pair can conflict at all unless each branch touches 100% of the file's lines
items.explanation: More lines touched by each side raises the probability that some line falls in both change lists — directly increasing conflict odds.
items.reference:
Branch lifetime and risk
longer-lived branch
→ more lines touched
→ more time for others to touch the same lines
→ higher line-overlap odds

Why: This is a mechanical consequence of the merge procedure, not a rule of thumb without a cause.

items.prompt: Alex inserts a new line right after line 3; Sam inserts a different new line at that exact same spot. What determines whether this conflicts?
choices: Insertions never conflict with each other — only modifications to an existing line can
Both insertions are anchored to the same base line, so it follows the same same-anchor-different-content rule as a modified line
Whichever branch happens to merge first always wins silently, with no marker shown
Insertions at the same spot always conflict automatically, regardless of their actual content
items.explanation: Insertions are tracked anchored to the nearest surviving base line — two different insertions at the same anchor point follow the exact same conflict rule as two different edits to the same line.
items.reference:
Anchored insertions
a new line isn't 'in' the base file
so it's anchored to the nearest surviving base line
same logic applies: same anchor + different content → conflict

Why: Insertions are handled by the same per-line procedure as modifications — they just need an anchor point since they don't correspond to an existing base line.

items.prompt: Why can't an inserted line be tracked by its own line number in the base file the way a modification can?
choices: It could be tracked that way, git just chooses not to for raw performance reasons
An inserted line doesn't correspond to any existing base line — it has to be anchored relative to a line that does still exist
Insertions are actually stored by git in a completely separate file from the rest of the content
Line numbers are irrelevant to how git tracks any change, insertion or otherwise
items.explanation: A brand-new line has no position in the original base file, so it has to be described relative to a base line it sits next to, rather than by an index into the base itself.
items.reference:
Anchored insertions
a new line isn't 'in' the base file
so it's anchored to the nearest surviving base line
same logic applies: same anchor + different content → conflict

Why: Insertions are handled by the same per-line procedure as modifications — they just need an anchor point since they don't correspond to an existing base line.
